# TriageX

**Every ER capacity tool shows you the problem. TriageX calls the people who can fix it.**

TriageX is an emergency department surge forecasting and active coordination demo built for the
Healthcare Track at Emory Hacks 2026. It pairs a deterministic surge simulation of a five-hospital
Metro Atlanta network with human-approved staffing outreach and patient level-loading, then shows
the modeled before-versus-after outcome.

> **Synthetic hospital operations simulation — not real-time hospital data.**
> Hospital names and locations are used only for geographic context. Every operational figure is
> synthetic. No hospital has supplied data to, approved, or partnered with this project, and TriageX
> is not a clinically validated operations platform.

## Status

| Area | State |
|---|---|
| Deterministic surge simulation (I-85 pileup, seed 42) | Complete, tested |
| FastAPI API + WebSocket, command-center dashboard | Complete, tested |
| Tiger Data persistence (TimescaleDB hypertable) | Complete; migrations 001–005 applied to the live service |
| FaceTime agent (Chert + LiveKit + Gemini Live), real caller video | Verified on real calls |
| Staff-card reading from live FaceTime video | Verified on a real call (5 cards, blank page) |
| Card → roster check → spoken "I confirm" → dashboard | Built and tested end to end over HTTP; full live call pending |
| iMessage on the Chert hackathon line | Built (mocked tests); key accepted by Chert; live round trip pending |
| Grounded AI operational brief (Gemini, template fallback) | Verified against the real Gemini API |

Evidence and open items: [docs/chert-status.md](docs/chert-status.md). The demo:
[docs/demo-script.md](docs/demo-script.md). API: [docs/api.md](docs/api.md). Plan and
assumptions: [docs/plan.md](docs/plan.md), [docs/assumptions.md](docs/assumptions.md).

## Try the simulation

```bash
cd backend
uv run python -m app.simulation.cli i85_pileup --seed 42
uv run python -m app.simulation.cli heat_wave --seed 7 --staff 0 --no-level-loading
```

## Layout

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `backend/` | FastAPI app, simulation engine, integrations, tests (Python 3.12, uv) |
| `frontend/` | React + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind dashboard |
| `agent/` | Chert FaceTime agent (Node, LiveKit Agents, Gemini Live + Gemini vision) |
| `db/migrations/` | Plain SQL migrations for Tiger Data |
| `docs/` | Handoff, plan, assumptions, demo script, status, printable test cards |
| `scripts/` | Dev and verification scripts |

## Prerequisites (macOS)

- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (installs Python 3.12 for the backend)
- **Node.js 24** (`/opt/homebrew/opt/node@24/bin` first on `PATH`; Homebrew's Node 25 is broken)
- An iPhone verified for the Chert project, and the Chert CLI via `npx @trychert/facetime@0.1.0-beta.21`

## Setup

```bash
cp .env.example .env                                 # backend keys (see below)
cp agent/.env.example agent/.env.local && chmod 600 agent/.env.local
(cd backend && uv sync)
(cd frontend && npm install)
(cd agent && npm install)
```

Keys (never commit them or paste them anywhere): the repo `.env` holds `DATABASE_URL` (optional),
`TRIAGEX_AGENT_TOKEN` (same value as in `agent/.env.local`; `openssl rand -hex 32`),
`GEMINI_API_KEY` (AI brief), and for iMessage `CHERT_API_KEY`, `CHERT_PROJECT_ID`,
`CHERT_LINE_ID` (`cd backend && uv run python ../scripts/chert_inspect.py`) and
`DEMO_ALLOWED_PHONES`. `agent/.env.local` holds the LiveKit keys, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`,
`TRIAGEX_AGENT_TOKEN` and `AGENT_NAME`. Every integration works without its keys and says so.

## Run (four terminals)

```bash
cd backend && uv run uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
cd frontend && npm run dev                      # http://localhost:5173
cd agent && npm start
cd agent && npx --yes @trychert/facetime@0.1.0-beta.21 dev --agent triagex-facetime-agent --minutes 30
```

Stop `chert dev` only with Ctrl+C and wait for "Stopped". The dashboard proxies `/api` and `/ws`
to `127.0.0.1:8000`; the API docs are at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. On Windows,
`scripts/dev.ps1` starts the backend and the dashboard.

## Test

```bash
cd backend && uv run pytest -q && uv run ruff check .     # DB tests start a local PostgreSQL
cd frontend && npm test && npm run lint && npm run build
cd agent && npm test
```

Rehearsal (needs the backend and `npm run dev` running; Chrome on macOS, Edge elsewhere):

```bash
cd frontend
npm run rehearse -- /tmp/rehearsal 1366 768                          # simulated replies
REHEARSE_CONFIRM=agent npm run rehearse -- /tmp/rehearsal 1366 768   # agent API, no phone
REHEARSE_CONFIRM=live  npm run rehearse -- /tmp/rehearsal 1366 768   # waits for a real call / iMessage
```

# TriageX — Devpost submission draft

**Category to select:** Best Use of FaceTime (Chert). Also the Healthcare track.

**Tagline:** Every ER capacity tool shows you the problem. TriageX calls the people who can fix it.

> **Synthetic data statement.** TriageX is a hackathon demo. Every hospital figure, patient, staff
> member and staff card is synthetic or fictional. Hospital names are used only for geographic
> context; no hospital supplied data to, approved or partnered with this project, and TriageX is
> not a clinically validated tool. No camera image is ever stored, and no phone number is stored.

## Inspiration

When a highway pileup sends a wave of ambulances to one emergency department, the dashboards
light up red, and then a charge nurse starts phoning people. Capacity tools are good at showing
the problem. The part that changes the outcome — getting qualified staff on the floor in time —
still runs on phone trees. We wanted the system that predicts the surge to also do the calling,
verify who answered, and show what that response is worth.

## What it does

1. **Predicts the surge.** A deterministic simulation of five Atlanta emergency departments runs
   an I-85 pileup scenario and forecasts each hospital's occupancy two hours ahead. TriageX
   proposes calling in staff where the forecast breaches capacity.
2. **A human approves.** Nothing is automatic. The approval starts a realistic 45-minute
   lead time.
3. **FaceTime does the verification.** A teammate FaceTimes the TriageX line. Our agent answers,
   tells them what is needed, and asks them to hold up their (fictional) staff card. It reads the
   card from the **live caller video**, and TriageX checks it against the roster: an unknown ID
   or an off-duty nurse is rejected out loud; a valid card is accepted only after the caller
   explicitly says "I confirm". The confirmation lands on the command-center dashboard within
   a fraction of a second.
4. **Two futures diverge.** The same patients, the same emergency: one future without TriageX,
   one with the confirmed staff arriving at 17:15. With three confirmations the demo window loses
   16.25 instead of 25.5 ambulance-hours to handoff delays (−36%), and the hospital recovers
   45 minutes sooner.
5. **iMessage and a grounded brief.** Staff can also confirm by replying IN to a "TriageX DEMO"
   iMessage, and an AI operational brief summarizes the situation using only numbers the
   simulation produced.

## How we built it

- **Simulation and API:** Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, a deterministic tick-based engine
  (seeded), WebSocket updates. A confirmation re-simulates only the TriageX future, so the
  baseline never moves.
- **Dashboard:** React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, Recharts. The playhead reveals data only up
  to the current simulated time, so nothing is spoiled early.
- **Tiger Data:** PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB stores runs, per-tick hospital metrics (a hypertable),
  confirmations, FaceTime calls, card checks and briefs.
- **Chert FaceTime API + LiveKit:** Chert bridges a real FaceTime Video call into a LiveKit room;
  our Node agent (LiveKit Agents) speaks with **Gemini Live** and publishes an animated face.
- **Seeing the card:** the agent samples at most one caller frame per second, crops the centre
  (dropping FaceTime's controls and self-view), downsizes it to a grayscale image in memory, and
  asks **Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite** for strict JSON (card present, ID, name, role, availability,
  confidence). A card counts only when two consecutive frames agree with confidence ≥ 0.8.
- **The backend decides.** The agent only extracts fields. FastAPI validates the card against a
  synthetic roster and records the confirmation exactly once, through the same code path as every
  other confirmation. "I confirm" is checked on the caller's own transcribed words, not on the
  voice model's judgement.
- **Chert iMessage:** the hackathon line's shared-messages API, polled while a reply is awaited.
- **Grounded AI brief:** Gemini writes text with `{metric_key}` placeholders only; the server
  fills in every number and rejects any digit or spelled-out number the model writes, with a
  fallback model and a deterministic template.

## Challenges

- **Free-tier latency and quotas.** Gemini answered in 1 s or in 50 s, and the free tier allows
  15 requests a minute per model. We pipeline requests, drop results overtaken by newer frames,
  and budget requests so the quota is never hit mid-call.
- **Temperature 0 was slow.** On some images it took 20–60 s; the default temperature took 1.5 s.
- **Not trusting the model.** Recognition needs two agreeing frames; validity is decided by the
  backend; confirmation needs the caller's actual words; the brief cannot write a number itself.
- **Video realities:** muted cameras, replaced tracks, glare, FaceTime UI in the frame, and
  stale frames — the agent never reuses an old frame.

## Accomplishments

- On a real FaceTime call the agent read five different cards with the exact ID and reported
  "no card" for a blank screen.
- The full card → roster → confirmation → dashboard path runs in well under a second after the
  confirmation; the baseline is provably unchanged.
- Hundreds of automated tests across the simulation, API, agent and dashboard.

## What we learned

Live video is a verification channel, not decoration — but only if every step that matters is
checked by deterministic code rather than by the model.

## What's next

- The agent places the call itself (outbound FaceTime) the moment an operator approves.
- QR codes on cards as a deterministic second signal.
- Real rosters and shift systems, with identity verification beyond a card.
- Patient-facing navigation (deliberately cut from this MVP).

## Built with

Python · FastAPI · Pydantic · uv · React · TypeScript · Vite · Tailwind CSS · Recharts ·
Tiger Data (PostgreSQL, TimescaleDB) · Chert FaceTime API · Chert iMessage · LiveKit Agents ·
Gemini Live · Gemini API (3.5 Flash-Lite vision, 3.1 Flash-Lite brief) · Playwright · Node.js

## 1. Executive summary

TriageX is a working, tested demo of an emergency-department surge forecasting and staff-coordination
system for five modeled Atlanta hospitals. A deterministic simulation runs the same synthetic surge
twice: once **without TriageX** (the baseline) and once **with TriageX**, where a forecast proposes
calling in staff, a human approves, staff confirm, and the confirmed staff arrive after a 45-minute
simulated lead time. A React command-center dashboard plays the two futures side by side, and every
run is stored in Tiger Data (PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB).

**What works today (on GitHub, tested):** the simulation engine, the FastAPI API and WebSocket, Tiger
Data persistence, and the dashboard with a clearly labeled *simulated* staff-reply fallback.

**What exists but is not live-verified:** a Chert **iMessage** integration (outbound "TriageX DEMO"
message, signed inbound webhook, deduplication, expiry, Tiger Data event tables). It is fully tested
with signed fixtures and a faked Chert HTTP API, but it has **never sent a real message**, and it
targets Chert's *console* messaging API, which is probably **not** the API used by the free
hackathon line.

**What is not started:** the **FaceTime agent** (the sponsor-prize centerpiece), the dashboard work
for live channels, and the AI operational brief (Phase 5).

**Your goal:** a real FaceTime call in which the TriageX agent sees a fictional staff card through the
iPhone camera, checks it against a synthetic roster, asks for explicit confirmation, and records the
confirmation through the existing backend so the two futures diverge after the 45-minute lead time.

### 1.1 Final scope decisions (agreed by the team, 2026-11-14)

The core product does not change. TriageX remains an AI-powered emergency-department surge response
system: it predicts overcrowding, recommends interventions, obtains human approval, coordinates
staffing, and demonstrates the impact through a deterministic simulation.

1. **Keep unchanged:** the simulation, Tiger Data integration, FastAPI backend, dashboard, and the
   baseline-versus-TriageX comparison.
2. **Chert FaceTime extends the existing staff outreach and confirmation workflow.** It is not a
   separate product.
3. **The FaceTime agent:**
   - uses genuine live video to read a fictional staff availability card;
   - checks it against a synthetic roster;
   - obtains explicit verbal confirmation;
   - triggers the existing staffing confirmation service.
4. **iMessage stays** as a practical staffing channel and as the fallback.
5. **Patient navigation** was a secondary, text-based feature in the original brief and was
   deliberately cut from the MVP. It is documented as future work (Section 16).
6. **Patient-facing FaceTime and visual injury assessment** are new, unimplemented proposals. Do not
   build them during the hackathon, and do not present them as original requirements.
7. **The simulation's underlying logic must not be modified** to accommodate FaceTime.

# TriageX API (Phase 3)

This is the backend contract for the single-screen command center. Every number in a
response is computed by the deterministic simulation; the frontend never calculates
deltas or percentages itself.

- Base URL in development: `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Use `127.0.0.1`, not `localhost`. On
  Windows, `localhost` tries IPv6 first and adds about 200 ms to every request.
- The Vite dev server proxies `/api` and `/ws` to the backend.
- Interactive schema: `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` (OpenAPI).

## Demo flow in four calls

| Step | Call | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Reset | `POST /api/demo/reset` | Fresh I-85 run, seed 42. Both futures are identical. |
| 2. Approve outreach | `POST /api/runs/{run_id}/proposals/{proposal_id}/approve` with `{"at_tick": <playhead tick>}` | Creates a staffing request. No outcome changes yet. |
| 3. Staff confirms (repeat) | `POST /api/runs/{run_id}/staffing-requests/{request_id}/simulate-reply` | Adds one confirmation and recalculates Track B. |
| 4. Read diagnostics (optional) | `GET /api/runs/{run_id}/diagnostics` | Engineering detail for judge Q&A. |

Every `POST` returns the complete `DashboardState`, so the screen re-renders from the
response without another request.

For step 2, use the card with `recommended: true` in `proposals`. Send `at_tick`, the
simulated tick at which the operator clicked Approve (the playhead position).

- `at_tick` is required. The server never assumes the approval happened at the proposal
  tick.
- It must be no earlier than the proposal tick.
- The 45-minute staffing lead time starts at `at_tick`.

In step 3, each confirmation counts in the simulation from the approval tick plus 45
simulated minutes. That holds no matter when the reply arrives in real time. History is
never rewritten: ticks before that point are identical in both tracks.

I-85 example timeline:

| Event | Simulated time |
|---|---|
| Surge Predicted | 16:15 |
| Outreach Approved (`at_tick` 18) | 16:30 |
| Staff en route (lead-time band) | 16:30–17:15 |
| Shift Active, Futures Diverge | 17:15 |

A request reports `proposal_clock`, `approved_clock` and `effective_clock`. Feed events
for confirmations sit at the approval tick, inside the lead-time band.

Measured on the development laptop (live uvicorn, curl, 5 rounds × 3 replies):

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| One confirmation, full HTTP round trip | 25.7–28.2 ms (about 12 ms recalculating Track B, 4–6 ms building the payload, the rest serialization and transport) |
| Reset | about 47 ms |

The payload is about 245 KB uncompressed and about 12 KB with gzip.

# TriageX FaceTime agent

Chert's video starter (`chert new agent --video`, @trychert/facetime 0.1.0-beta.21), adapted for
TriageX. All data is synthetic. Differences from the starter:

- **Voice model:** Gemini Live via `@livekit/agents-plugin-google` 1.8.0 (free tier of the Gemini
  API, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`) instead of OpenAI realtime. Model:
  `gemini-2.5-flash-native-audio-preview-12-2025`, overridable with `GEMINI_LIVE_MODEL`.
- **Staff-card reading** (`card-session.mjs`, `card-reader.mjs`, `frame-utils.mjs`, `vision.mjs`):
  while a scan is active ("awaiting card"), at most one frame per second from the caller's
  `facetime-remote-video` track is centre-cropped (80 %, dropping FaceTime controls and self-preview),
  downscaled to a 1024 px grayscale PNG **in memory**, and sent to `VISION_MODEL`
  (default `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, same `GOOGLE_API_KEY`) with a strict JSON schema. A reading is
  accepted only when the same `card_id` comes back in 2 consecutive samples with confidence ≥ 0.8;
  otherwise the agent asks the caller (by voice) to hold the card closer, steadier, out of glare, or to
  turn the camera on. A scan times out after 45 s. The scan starts with the greeting; the caller can ask
  to scan again (`scan_staff_card` tool). Logs are `[card]` lines with text fields only; no frame is ever
  written to disk. **The agent only extracts fields; the backend validates cards (Prompt 4).**
- **Why a separate vision call:** `@livekit/agents-plugin-google` 1.8.0 does not forward video to
  Gemini Live (`pushVideo` is a no-op), so the voice model never sees the camera.
- **Frame probe:** `frame-probe.mjs` (Stage C evidence) now runs only with `FRAME_PROBE=1`.
- **Tests:** `npm test` (Node's built-in runner; recorded model outputs in `test/fixtures/`, no images).
- **Roster check and confirmation** (`backend.mjs`, Prompt 4): after a stable reading the agent
  sends the fields to the TriageX backend (`BACKEND_URL`, header `X-TriageX-Agent-Token` =
  `TRIAGEX_AGENT_TOKEN`), which decides validity against the synthetic roster. The agent says the
  result; for a valid card it asks the caller to say "I confirm". That phrase is checked on the
  caller's own words (Gemini Live input transcription, `isConfirmation`), never left to the voice
  model; only then does the backend record one confirmation. A rejected card re-arms the scanner
  for a different card. Without the token the agent only reads cards.

Run (Node 24): `npm start` in one terminal; in a second terminal, from this folder,
`npx --yes @trychert/facetime@0.1.0-beta.21 dev --agent triagex-facetime-agent --minutes 30`.
Then FaceTime Video the line. Status and evidence: [../docs/chert-status.md](../docs/chert-status.md).

A voice agent with a face, for FaceTime Video calls through Chert. It is the voice

# TriageX Database (Phase 4: Tiger Data)

TriageX stores every demo run in PostgreSQL and uses TimescaleDB, which Tiger Data
provides, for the per-tick hospital time series. Every stored value is synthetic
simulation output.

## Setup

1. Create a Tiger Data service and copy its connection string.
2. Put the connection string in the repo-root `.env` file (never committed):

   ```
   DATABASE_URL=postgres://tsdbadmin:<password>@<service>.tsdb.cloud.timescale.com:<port>/tsdb?sslmode=require
   ```

3. Apply the migrations and run the end-to-end check:

   ```powershell
   cd backend
   uv run python ../scripts/migrate.py      # safe to repeat
   uv run python ../scripts/verify_db.py    # prints VERIFIED only if every check passes
   ```

4. Start the API as usual. It connects and migrates in the background, so startup
   never waits for the database.

Without `DATABASE_URL` the app runs fully in memory. In that case
`/api/integrations/health` reports the database as `not_configured`, never `ok`.

**Driver:** the app uses `pg8000`, a pure-Python PostgreSQL driver. Windows Application
Control on the demo laptop blocks psycopg's native libpq DLL.

**TLS:** `sslmode` follows libpq. `require` encrypts the connection without checking the
certificate; `verify-full` checks it.

## Schema

The schema lives in `db/migrations/` and is applied in order by
`app/repositories/migrations.py`. Each migration is recorded with a checksum in
`schema_migrations`.

> [!IMPORTANT] > **Synthetic hospital operations simulation, not real-time hospital data.** Hospital names and > locations are used only for geographic context. Every operational figure, patient, staff member > and staff card is synthetic or fictional. No hospital has supplied data to, approved, or partnered > with this project, and TriageX is not a clinically validated operations platform. No camera image > and no phone number is ever stored. --- ## The problem When a highway pileup sends a wave of ambulances to one emergency department, the dashboards turn red, and then a charge nurse starts phoning people. Capacity tools are good at *showing* the surge. The step that changes the outcome, getting qualified staff on the floor in time, still runs on phone trees. TriageX connects the forecast to the response. It predicts the surge, proposes a staffing intervention, waits for a human to approve it, reaches staff over **FaceTime** and **iMessage**, verifies who answered, and shows what that response is worth by running the same emergency twice. ## What it does | | Step | What happens | |---|---|---| | 1 | **Predict** | A deterministic simulation of five Metro Atlanta EDs runs an I-85 pileup and forecasts each hospital's occupancy two hours ahead. Where the forecast breaches capacity, TriageX proposes calling in staff. | | 2 | **Approve** | Nothing is automatic. An operator approves the proposal, which starts a realistic 45-minute staffing lead time. | | 3 | **Verify on FaceTime** | A staff member FaceTimes the TriageX line. The agent explains the request and asks them to hold up their staff card. It reads the card from the **live caller video**; the backend checks it against the roster. Unknown or off-duty cards are rejected out loud. A valid card counts only after the caller says *"I confirm"*. | | 4 | **Compare two futures** | Same patients, same emergency. One future without TriageX, one with the confirmed staff arriving at 17:15. | | 5 | **Brief** | Staff can also confirm by replying `IN` over iMessage, and a grounded AI brief summarizes the situation using only numbers the simulation produced. | ### Result on the I-85 pileup scenario (seed 42) | Metric | Without TriageX | With TriageX | Change | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Ambulance-hours lost to handoff delays (15:00–20:45) | 25.50 h | **16.25 h** | **−9.25 h (−36%)** | | Focus hospital recovery | | **45 min sooner** | | | Confirmation → dashboard update | | **< 100 ms** | | ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Caller["📱 Staff member"] FT["FaceTime Video"] IM["iMessage"] end subgraph Chert["Chert"] Bridge["FaceTime bridge"] Line["Shared iMessage line"] end subgraph Agent["agent/ · Node 24"] LK["LiveKit Agents worker"] Voice["Gemini Live

Gemini returns text with `{metric_key}` placeholders, the server fills in every value from the simulation, and any digit or spelled-out number in the model output is rejected. The chain falls back from the primary model to a second model and then to a deterministic template, and the dashboard shows which one produced the brief. ```mermaid flowchart LR State["Dashboard state at the playhead"] --> Primary["Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite"] Primary -->|"timeout / invalid"| Fallback["Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite"] Fallback -->|"timeout / invalid"| Template["Deterministic template"] Primary --> Check{"No numbers written
by the model?"} Fallback --> Check Check -->|yes| Fill["Server fills {metric_key} placeholders"] Check -->|no| Template Template --> Fill --> Out["Brief + source label"] ``` ### Data model Every run is stored in Tiger Data. Per-tick hospital metrics live in a TimescaleDB hypertable. ```mermaid erDiagram simulation_runs ||--o{ run_versions : has simulation_runs ||--o{ hospital_metrics : "per tick (hypertable)" simulation_runs ||--o{ comparison_metrics : has simulation_runs ||--o{ staffing_requests : has staffing_requests ||--o{ staff_confirmations : receives staffing_requests ||--o{ outreach_events : sends staffing_requests ||--o{ facetime_calls : "answered by" facetime_calls ||--o{ card_checks : performs simulation_runs ||--o{ ai_briefs : has simulation_runs ||--o{ intervention_events : logs hospitals ||--o{ hospital_metrics : measured scenarios ||--o{ simulation_runs : drives ``` ## Design principles - **Human in the loop.** The system proposes; a person approves. ## 1. Executive summary

TriageX is a working, tested demo of an emergency-department surge forecasting and staff-coordination
system for five modeled Atlanta hospitals. A deterministic simulation runs the same synthetic surge
twice: once **without TriageX** (the baseline) and once **with TriageX**, where a forecast proposes
calling in staff, a human approves, staff confirm, and the confirmed staff arrive after a 45-minute
simulated lead time. A React command-center dashboard plays the two futures side by side, and every
run is stored in Tiger Data (PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB).

**What works today (on GitHub, tested):** the simulation engine, the FastAPI API and WebSocket, Tiger
Data persistence, and the dashboard with a clearly labeled *simulated* staff-reply fallback.

**What exists but is not live-verified:** a Chert **iMessage** integration (outbound "TriageX DEMO"
message, signed inbound webhook, deduplication, expiry, Tiger Data event tables). It is fully tested
with signed fixtures and a faked Chert HTTP API, but it has **never sent a real message**, and it
targets Chert's *console* messaging API, which is probably **not** the API used by the free
hackathon line.

**What is not started:** the **FaceTime agent** (the sponsor-prize centerpiece), the dashboard work
for live channels, and the AI operational brief (Phase 5).

**Your goal:** a real FaceTime call in which the TriageX agent sees a fictional staff card through the
iPhone camera, checks it against a synthetic roster, asks for explicit confirmation, and records the
confirmation through the existing backend so the two futures diverge after the 45-minute lead time.

"""Development provenance for the technical panel: the running commit and the Entire
checkpoint refs stored in the repository. Read-only; reports what git returns."""

from __future__ import annotations

import subprocess

from fastapi import APIRouter

from app.config import ENGINE_VERSION, REPO_ROOT

router = APIRouter(tags=["meta"])


def _git(*args: str) -> str | None:
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(
            ["git", *args], cwd=REPO_ROOT, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5, check=True
        )
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        return None
    return out.stdout.strip()


@router.get("/meta/provenance")
def provenance() -> dict:
    refs = _git("for-each-ref", "--format=%(refname)", "refs/entire/checkpoints") or ""
    checkpoints = sorted(r.rsplit("/", 1)[-1] for r in refs.splitlines() if r)
    return {
        "engine_version": ENGINE_VERSION,
        "commit": _git("rev-parse", "HEAD"),
        "commit_subject": _git("log", "-1", "--format=%s"),
        "branch": _git("rev-parse", "--abbrev-ref", "HEAD"),
        "entire_checkpoints": checkpoints,
        "entire_checkpoint_count": len(checkpoints),
        "source": "git" if refs or checkpoints else "git (no Entire checkpoint refs found)",
    }

## Built with Entire

TriageX was built phase by phase with Claude Code, and [Entire](https://entire.io) recorded every
session as a checkpoint linked to the commits it produced. The reasoning behind the code is
versioned alongside the code, so anyone can see why a change was made, not just what changed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Session["Claude Code session"] -->|"hooks: start · prompt · stop · end"| Entire["Entire CLI"]
    Entire -->|checkpoint| Refs["refs/entire/* git refs"]
    Commit["git commit"] --> Refs
    Refs -->|push| GitHub["GitHub origin"]
    Refs -->|"GET /api/meta/provenance"| Panel["Dashboard technical panel"]
```

- **Checkpoints stored as git refs** (`.entire/settings.json`, `"type": "git-refs"`) and pushed to
  `origin` with the code, so no separate service is needed to read them.
- **Automatic capture.** Claude Code hooks in [.claude/settings.json](.claude/settings.json) call
  `entire` at session start, on each prompt, on stop and at session end.
- **Provenance in the product.** `GET /api/meta/provenance`
  ([backend/app/api/meta.py](backend/app/api/meta.py)) reports the running commit and the Entire
  checkpoint refs, and the dashboard's technical panel shows them during the demo.
- **Handoffs that keep context.** A teammate continuing on another machine fetches the history and
  can ask what any past session did:

```bash
git fetch origin 'refs/entire/*:refs/entire/*'
entire checkpoint list
entire checkpoint explain <id>
```
